routeSelection.basis: The generic target has two equally formal 54-EC specialisations, Landscape Architecture and Spatial Planning. Neither is identified as the general route, so the first current handbook specialisation is selected neutrally and independently of UCR fit.

alternatives.label: Landscapes, water & spatial sustainability
alternatives.concept: Combines landscape-forming processes, soil and water, ecology, GIS and nature-based interventions with social inquiry, visual analysis and policy. The emphasis is on understanding places and evaluating sustainable spatial responses.
alternatives.labelReason: Combines landscape-forming processes, soil and water, ecology, GIS and nature-based interventions with social inquiry, visual analysis and policy. The emphasis is on understanding places and evaluating sustainable spatial responses.
progression: All formal prerequisites precede their dependent courses, and every course has a planned offering in its assigned term. Relevant scientific and social-research foundations support later applications. Each plan has 24 unique courses, four per term, Year-1 PPD and at least six 300-level courses.
alternatives.distinctness: The broad response integrates physical landscape evidence with social and visual analysis. It differs by 7 courses from the ecology route and 8 from the governance route.

core: Landscape architecture, spatial planning, place and regional design
Ecology, soils, water, climate and landscape processes
Planning governance, land-use conflict, law, economics and participation
Landscape meaning, visualisation and spatial evidence
Planning and design theory, studios, research methods and thesis work
adjacent: Landscape ecology, climate adaptation and spatial evidence

questions: How can spatial plans balance competing social, environmental and economic interests?
How can people, institutions and participation shape sustainable places?

selection.assessment: The closest response materially addresses landscape processes, geospatial evidence and nature-based interventions, with human, economic and visual evaluation. A second response prioritises ecological mechanisms and quantitative environmental evidence; only after accepting it is a third response accepted with socio-legal, governance and participation priorities. All are coherent, feasible and substantively distinct. Professional landscape design, planting/construction representation and repeated studios remain major gaps. Stop at the three-alternative maximum without presenting any UCR route as equivalent professional landscape-architecture training.

trace: Complementary physics, chemistry, elementary calculus and dynamic modelling give scientific tools for understanding environmental processes underlying landscape interventions.
Complementary markets, incentives and economic allocation provide foundations for reasoning about competing land uses and public intervention.
Complementary analysis of social structures, groups, inequality and identity supports understanding whose interests and experiences shape decisions about places.

Complementary waves, chemical analysis, material structure and stress/strain support geospatial observation and material/environmental reasoning; it also supplies the formal foundation for Spatial Planning and remediation.

Direct institutional and stakeholder analysis of food, water, energy and climate governance, with a real Zeeland issue, consultation and policy advice/evaluation; supports participatory environmental decisions, not full planning-studio equivalence.
Direct qualitative research design, interviewing, observation, reflexivity and coding support stakeholder/community inquiry about environmental and spatial decisions.
Direct research-design, survey, sampling and statistical inference/regression foundations support evidence-based analysis of human-environment questions.
Direct geology, geomorphology and Earth-system processes explain the landforms and physical conditions to which landscape interventions respond.
Direct climate impacts, agriculture, justice and governance analysis supports adaptation-oriented decisions; stakeholder inquiry connects scientific and social evidence.
Direct biodiversity and organismal/ecological foundations support understanding living systems and the ecological effects of land interventions.
Direct nature-based intervention design: ecological connectivity and infrastructure projects examine how constructed responses can work with coastal, river and urban ecosystems.
Direct GIS and remote-sensing investigation: spatial data, projections, map/surface analysis and environmental case studies provide spatial evidence for decisions about places.
Direct soil and groundwater investigation explains land-use capacity, water movement and contamination relevant to landscape analysis and intervention constraints.

Direct geospatial engineering and GIS/remote-sensing projects address disasters, agriculture, resources and pollution. Its actual description supports spatial environmental applications; it does not establish land-use law, professional planning theory or landscape studio training.
Direct public-goods, externalities, welfare, expenditure and distribution analysis supports economic appraisal of environmental public intervention; no specialist land-valuation model is invented.
Direct analysis of contaminated environments, recycling, recovery and remediation supports evaluation of land/water restoration interventions and their material trade-offs.
Direct analysis of environmental chemical and biogeochemical processes supports understanding nutrient/contaminant pathways and the consequences of land and water interventions.
Complementary comparative institutions, political participation and policy processes support analysis of who makes spatial/environmental decisions and how representation works.

Complementary close visual analysis of composition, space, form, tone and colour supplies artistic/visual evaluation relevant to landscape representation. Painting analysis is not landscape drawing, design practice or environmental aesthetic theory.
Direct site-based delta inquiry connects flood risk, freshwater, salinisation, infrastructure and ecological consequences to context-sensitive adaptation strategies.
Direct conservation biology examines biodiversity decline, fragmentation and conservation responses, supporting biodiversity-sensitive spatial choices.
Direct Earth-system measurement and analysis tools support empirical investigation of environmental conditions; this is environmental methods training rather than a dedicated landscape-design studio.
Direct policy-process analysis using a sugar case across national/international arenas, with policy memos; supports structured policy argument without claiming zoning or planning-law instruction.

Complementary life-cycle assessment evaluates resource extraction, environmental impacts, reuse and costs of products/processes; supports appraisal of material interventions without claiming construction-detail training.
Direct data integration, exploratory analysis and visualisation, including spatial data, support investigation and communication of environmental evidence.
Complementary population variation, adaptation, speciation, biogeography and extinction explain biodiversity processes important to the ecological route; no landscape-design methods are claimed.
Direct predictive modelling, validation and uncertainty-aware data analysis support the quantitative ecological/spatial-investigation direction.
Direct ecosystem processes, communities and interactions provide ecological evidence for evaluating land-use impacts and restoration.
Direct comparison of farming practices and their ecosystem/environmental impacts supports investigation of rural land-use alternatives and sustainable production landscapes.
Direct study of geological resources, extraction and environmental consequences supports appraisal of resource pressures and material choices affecting landscapes.

Complementary Indigenous histories of dispossession, ecological knowledge, food sovereignty and cultural continuity provide a concrete historical case of relationships between land, identity and power.
Complementary critical social theory about modernity, colonial relations, stigma and intersecting inequalities informs analysis of power and inclusion in planning decisions.
Direct rhetorical analysis, public argument, debate and storytelling prepare communication of contested environmental and spatial proposals.
Direct environmental justice, social movements, decolonial approaches and degrowth support inquiry into contested land use and participation.
Complementary legal and socio-legal foundations, property/public law and justice prepare examination of institutions and legal constraints; formal prerequisite for Comparative Constitutional Law.
Complementary advanced analysis of civil society, solidarity, trust and collective movements supports understanding organised participation and collective action around places.
Direct persuasion and framing with sustainability/community applications support communicating proposals and participating in public environmental decisions.

Direct comparative constitutional/administrative institutions, public participation, remedies and procedural fairness support the legal-governance side of planning; no dedicated Dutch planning-law course is claimed.
blocks: Shared elementary differentiation/integration and dynamic models; WUR dedicates its course to calculus and differential equations, while UCR embeds these tools in physical/environmental science.
Shared geological and geomorphological processes forming landscapes; WUR integrates Dutch hydrology, soils, land use, vegetation and historical landscape identity more broadly.
Shared soils, groundwater and land-use constraints; WUR includes its own geology/soil-landscape field excursion.
Shared ecological principles, ecosystem processes and interactions; WUR provides a compact introductory ecology foundation.

Shared applied investigation of a concrete environmental/place issue, stakeholder interests and proposed intervention advice; WUR additionally produces a spatial/action plan through an intensive field-based planning studio.
Shared analysis of place and nature-based intervention proposals; WUR provides a full landscape studio with a client brief, multiple scales and professional representational practice.
Shared public goods, externalities, economic policy and distribution; WUR specifically applies economics and politics to land use, locations and landscape value.
Shared understanding of water movement, quality and environmental relationships; UCR emphasises delta risks and adaptation rather than a global introductory hydrology survey.
Shared visual evaluation of space, form, colour and composition through art; WUR adds philosophical/environmental aesthetic frameworks and critique of landscape designs.
Shared investigation of land, cultural identity, historical power and contemporary uses; UCR provides an Indigenous North American case, not WUR’s broad cultural/historical landscape geography.
Shared research design, questions, qualitative data collection, observation and interviews; WUR develops a broader human-environment research proposal across study designs.
Shared estimation, testing and regression as foundations for empirical research.
Shared GIS, spatial data handling, cartography, terrain/surface analysis and remote-sensing methods with practical projects.
Shared science-informed practical investigation of spatial/environmental problems and intervention projects; WUR teaches integrated creative landscape planning/design beyond geospatial engineering.

notes.text: WUR combines landscape processes with repeated site, urban and regional design studios, planting, construction, representation, aesthetics and a research-based design thesis. UCR can address landscapes through substantial environmental and geospatial investigation, nature-based interventions, visual analysis and governance. The professional studio sequence, planting/construction detailing and design-thesis training remain major differences.

audience.programmeDescription: Landscape Architecture and Planning studies how people shape places for human and ecological needs. This Dutch-taught programme combines soil, water, ecology, geography and spatial evidence with planning and creative design. The example follows the Landscape Architecture specialisation.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programmes respond through landscape processes and nature-based interventions, ecological and spatial investigation, or land-use governance and participation. WUR offers much more sustained landscape design, studio practice, planting, construction and representation. UCR’s Spatial Planning course supports geospatial environmental applications; it does not replace that professional training.

curriculum.limitation: This 180-credit example contains 96 common credits, 42 taught specialisation credits, a 12-credit design thesis and 30 open credits. It assumes VWO Mathematics A preparation and completes the required taught study and safety preparation before the thesis.
